sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll have a working SQLite database connected to Claude Code via MCP — and you'll have used natural language to create tables, insert data, run queries, and explore a schema without writing a single line of SQL yourself.

## What SQLite Is

SQLite is a lightweight database that lives in a single file. Unlike PostgreSQL or MySQL, there's no server to set up, no service to run, no accounts to configure. The entire database is one `.db` file on your hard drive.

This makes it perfect for:
- Personal projects and scripts
- Learning how databases work
- Storing structured data that JSON or CSV doesn't handle well
- Prototyping database designs before scaling to a real server

SQLite is used in iOS apps, Android apps, browsers, and embedded systems. It's one of the most widely deployed database engines in the world.

## What the SQLite MCP Does

The SQLite MCP server exposes these tools to Claude:

- **`read_query`** — Run a SELECT query and return results
- **`write_query`** — Run INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL statements
- **`create_table`** — Create a new table with a schema
- **`list_tables`** — Show all tables in the database
- **`describe_table`** — Show the schema of a specific table
- **`append_insight`** — Log an observation about the data (for analysis workflows)

This means you can ask Claude 'which books have I read in the last 3 months?' and it writes the SQL, runs it, and returns the answer — no SQL knowledge required.

## Installation

Install the SQLite MCP server and add it to your configuration:
Add it to your global `settings.json`, replacing `YourName` with your actual Windows username:

**The database file path:** The last argument is the path to the `.db` file. If the file doesn't exist yet, the SQLite MCP will create it when Claude first tries to write to it. You don't need to create the file manually.

## How Claude Interacts With a Database

Here's what the experience looks like when you ask Claude a data question:

1. You ask: `"How many books have I read this year?"`
2. Claude calls `list_tables` to see what tables exist
3. Claude calls `describe_table` on the relevant table to see its schema
4. Claude writes the SQL: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE date_read >= '2026-01-01'`
5. Claude calls `read_query` with that SQL
6. The MCP server runs the query against your database file
7. Results come back: `[{"count": 7}]`
8. Claude reports: 'You've read 7 books so far this year.'

You never wrote SQL. You never looked at the schema. You just asked in plain English.

**SQL is still worth learning.** The SQLite MCP reduces the friction of working with data, but understanding basic SQL makes you a much better collaborator — you can catch when Claude writes an inefficient or incorrect query. Lesson 11 covers database concepts in more depth.

## Ideas for What to Store in SQLite

Some personal databases that are genuinely useful:

- **Book log** — title, author, date read, rating, notes
- **Movie tracker** — title, year, date watched, genre, rating
- **Habit tracker** — habit name, date, completed (1/0)
- **Expense log** — date, amount, category, description
- **Link library** — URL, title, category, date saved, notes
- **Recipe collection** — name, ingredients, instructions, cuisine, prep time

Once the data is in SQLite and Claude has access, you can ask questions like 'what's my average book rating by genre?' or 'how many habits did I complete last week?' — and get real answers instantly.

sections.title: Build a Personal Book Log Database
sections.content:
**Setup:**
1. Run `npm install -g @modelcontextprotocol/server-sqlite` in PowerShell
2. Add the sqlite entry to your `settings.json` (shown above)
3. Relaunch `claude`, type `/mcp` — confirm `sqlite` is listed

**Task 1 — Create the database:**
Ask: `"Using the SQLite MCP, create a table called 'books' with these columns:
- id (integer, primary key, auto-increment)
- title (text, required)
- author (text, required)
- genre (text)
- date_read (text, format: YYYY-MM-DD)
- rating (integer, 1–5)
- notes (text)"
`
Confirm it was created by asking: `"List all tables in the database and describe the books table schema."`

**Task 2 — Add real data:**
Ask: `"Add these 5 books to the database:
1. 'Deep Work' by Cal Newport, Non-Fiction, read 2026-01-15, rating 5
2. 'The Pragmatic Programmer' by Dave Thomas, Technology, read 2026-02-10, rating 4
3. 'Atomic Habits' by James Clear, Self-Help, read 2026-03-01, rating 5
4. 'The Phoenix Project' by Gene Kim, Technology, read 2026-04-20, rating 4
5. 'Thinking Fast and Slow' by Daniel Kahneman, Psychology, read 2026-05-05, rating 3"
`

**Task 3 — Query with natural language:**
Ask these questions one at a time and let Claude write and run the SQL:
- `"Show me all my books sorted by rating, highest first."`
- `"How many books have I read in each genre?"`
- `"What's my average rating across all books?"`
- `"Which books did I rate 5 stars?"`

**Task 4 — Add your own books:**
Ask: `"Add 3 books I've actually read recently."` and give Claude real titles and authors from books you've actually read. Add ratings you'd genuinely give them.

**Task 5 — Explore the schema:**
Ask: `"What's the SQL schema for the books table? Show me the CREATE TABLE statement."`

Note what it looks like — this is what Claude generated and executed on your behalf.

The database file `exercises/practice.db` now exists on your hard drive. You can open it with any SQLite browser (like DB Browser for SQLite, available free at sqlitebrowser.org) to see it visually.

sections.title: Workshop A — SQLite MCP First Queries
sections.content:
This drill gets you running real SQL queries via Claude Code.

**Step 1 — Set up a SQLite database** for testing:
```powershell
# Create a test database using Python
python -c "import sqlite3; conn = sqlite3.connect('test.db'); c = conn.cursor(); c.execute('CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT, created_at TEXT)'); c.executemany('INSERT INTO users VALUES (?,?,?,?)', [(1,'Alice','alice@example.com','2024-01-15'),(2,'Bob','bob@example.com','2024-02-20'),(3,'Carol','carol@example.com','2024-03-10')]); conn.commit()"
```

**Step 2 — Configure SQLite MCP** to point to test.db.

**Step 3 — In Claude Code**, run these queries:
- "List all tables in the database"
- "Show the schema for the users table"
- "Count how many users were created each month"
- "Find any users with duplicate email addresses"

**Step 4 — Ask Claude to write a query you don't know how to write:** "Find the users who were created most recently in each month."

**Step 5 — Verify all queries** return correct results.

sections.title: Workshop B — Real Database Analysis
sections.content:
Use SQLite MCP to analyse a real database from your work.

**Step 1 — Identify a real SQLite database** from your work (or create a small one from CSV data you have).

**Step 2 — Run a comprehensive database analysis:**
```
Analyse this database:
1. List all tables with their row counts
2. For each table, describe what it likely contains based on the schema
3. Identify foreign key relationships (even if not formally declared)
4. Find any tables that seem to have data quality issues (nulls, duplicates, anomalies)
5. What are the 3 most important business questions this database could answer?
```

**Step 3 — Ask the most important question** from Claude's analysis.

**Step 4 — Mandatory review:** Ask: *"Review your analysis. What assumptions did you make about the data that might be wrong? What would you need to verify to be confident in these findings?"*

**Step 5 — Create a one-page database documentation** based on Claude's analysis.

sections.title: Workshop C — Safe Database Operations
sections.content:
Practice running database operations with appropriate safety measures.

**Step 1 — Understand the risk tiers:**
- **Safe**: SELECT queries — read-only, no risk
- **Careful**: INSERT, UPDATE — adds or changes data
- **Dangerous**: DELETE, DROP — removes data permanently

**Step 2 — For any write operation**, always use this workflow:
1. Run a SELECT to see what you're about to change
2. Verify the WHERE clause would target exactly the right rows
3. Then run the write operation

**Step 3 — Practice the pattern:**
```
-- First: see what you're about to update
SELECT * FROM users WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';
-- Review the rows, then:
UPDATE users SET status = 'archived' WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';
```

**Step 4 — Ask Claude Code** to run an UPDATE on your test database using this workflow.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** "What database safety practices should I configure in CLAUDE.md to prevent Claude Code from running destructive database operations without confirmation?"

sections.title: Workshop D — AI-Generated SQL Reporting
sections.content:
Use Claude Code with SQLite MCP to generate automated data reports.

**Step 1 — Choose a reporting question** you regularly need answered from your data.

**Step 2 — Ask Claude Code to write and run the report:**
```
Generate a report answering: [your question]

For the report:
1. Write the SQL query
2. Explain what the query does before running it
3. Run the query
4. Interpret the results: what do the numbers mean?
5. What follow-up questions do the results raise?
```

**Step 3 — Review the SQL** before Claude Code runs it.

**Step 4 — Validate the results** against what you expect or can manually verify.

**Step 5 — Save the query** in a queries library for reuse. Ask Claude to format it with comments explaining each part.

sections.question: Claude Code generates this SQL: `DELETE FROM users WHERE last_login < '2023-01-01'`. Before executing it, what must you do?
options: Check if the database is backed up
Run `SELECT * FROM users WHERE last_login < '2023-01-01'` first to see exactly which rows will be deleted and verify this is your intent
Verify the SQL syntax is correct
Ask Claude Code if it's sure about the query
sections.explanation: Before any DELETE: always SELECT first with the same WHERE clause to see exactly what will be affected. This is the professional safety protocol. Even if Claude Code correctly understood your request, verify: are there really that many rows? Are any of these IDs in use in other tables? Is the date threshold right? A DELETE with no backup and no prior SELECT check is one of the most common paths to irreversible data loss.

sections.question: Claude Code writes an SQL query with a JOIN between tables and tells you it represents "all active users who made a purchase in 2024." Why might this still need verification?
options: Claude Code SQL is always correct
The JOIN logic might not match your database's actual foreign key structure, or "active" might be defined differently in your schema than Claude Code assumed
SQL JOINs are automatically validated by the database
The query will error if it's wrong, so errors will catch any issues
sections.explanation: Claude Code makes assumptions about schema relationships that may not match your actual data model. "Active users" might mean different things in different schemas (status = 'active', is_deleted = false, last_login within 30 days). The JOIN might use wrong column names or miss a required condition. Always check: does the WHERE clause match your actual definition? Does the row count make sense? Run with a LIMIT first on large tables.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 8-13.** You can now use natural language to interact with a real database. Lesson 8-14 covers how to find MCP servers beyond the ones covered in this course.
